entries.title: Ability Checks
entries.summary: An ability check tests a creature’s effort to overcome a challenge using one of the six abilities, sometimes with a skill or tool proficiency.
entries.whatItMeans: An ability check tests a creature’s effort to overcome a challenge using one of the six abilities, sometimes with a skill or tool proficiency.
entries.exampleInPlay: The Game Master calls for a Strength (Athletics) check when a character tries to force open a stuck gate.
entries.whyItMatters: Choosing the ability first and then any relevant proficiency keeps checks tied to what the character is actually doing.
commonMistakes: Players describe an approach; the Game Master decides whether a check is needed and which ability applies.

entries.title: Dice Notation
entries.summary: Dice notation shows how many dice to roll, what size they are, and which modifier to apply.
entries.whatItMeans: Dice notation shows how many dice to roll, what size they are, and which modifier to apply.
entries.exampleInPlay: 2d6 + 3 means roll two six-sided dice, add them together, and then add 3.
entries.whyItMatters: Reading notation quickly keeps play moving and prevents the modifier from being applied to every die by mistake.
commonMistakes: The number after the plus or minus sign is applied once unless a rule explicitly says otherwise.

entries.title: Difficulty Class
entries.summary: A Difficulty Class, usually shortened to DC, is the target number an ability check or saving throw must meet or exceed.
entries.whatItMeans: A Difficulty Class, usually shortened to DC, is the target number an ability check or saving throw must meet or exceed.
entries.exampleInPlay: A DC 15 check succeeds when the final total is 15 or higher.
entries.whyItMatters: The DC turns a fictional obstacle into a consistent numerical target.
commonMistakes: The DC is not subtracted from the roll; compare the final total directly with it.

entries.title: Expertise
entries.summary: Expertise doubles the proficiency bonus for a check that uses a chosen proficiency, subject to the feature that grants it.
entries.whatItMeans: Expertise doubles the proficiency bonus for a check that uses a chosen proficiency, subject to the feature that grants it.
entries.exampleInPlay: With a +3 proficiency bonus, Expertise contributes +6 before the ability modifier is added.
entries.whyItMatters: Expertise marks exceptional training and can make a character reliably strong in a focused area.
commonMistakes: Expertise doubles the proficiency bonus, not the entire check bonus.

entries.title: Group Checks
entries.summary: A group check measures whether a group succeeds together; the group normally succeeds when at least half of the participants succeed.
entries.whatItMeans: A group check measures whether a group succeeds together; the group normally succeeds when at least half of the participants succeed.
entries.exampleInPlay: Three of five adventurers succeed on a group Dexterity (Stealth) check, so the group succeeds.
entries.whyItMatters: Group checks prevent one weak roll from automatically ruining a task that the group is attempting collectively.

entries.title: Passive Checks
entries.summary: A passive check represents an average result without rolling, usually calculated as 10 plus the modifiers that would apply to the check.
entries.whatItMeans: A passive check represents an average result without rolling, usually calculated as 10 plus the modifiers that would apply to the check.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character with +4 Perception has a passive Perception score of 14 before other adjustments.
entries.whyItMatters: Passive checks let the Game Master resolve ongoing or hidden situations without repeatedly asking for dice rolls.
commonMistakes: A passive score is not a guaranteed minimum for every active check unless a rule says it is.

entries.title: Proficiency
entries.summary: Proficiency means a character is trained with a skill, saving throw, weapon, armor type, tool, or another game element.
entries.whatItMeans: Proficiency means a character is trained with a skill, saving throw, weapon, armor type, tool, or another game element.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character proficient in Stealth adds the proficiency bonus to a Dexterity (Stealth) check.
entries.whyItMatters: Proficiency is the main way training and class identity improve a character’s odds.
commonMistakes: The proficiency bonus is normally added only once to a roll, even when several sources grant proficiency.

entries.title: Rounding Numbers
entries.summary: When a rule tells you to divide a number and does not say otherwise, round down to the nearest whole number.
entries.whatItMeans: When a rule tells you to divide a number and does not say otherwise, round down to the nearest whole number.
entries.exampleInPlay: Half of 9 becomes 4 unless the rule specifically directs another result.
entries.whyItMatters: A single rounding convention prevents small calculations from producing inconsistent results.

entries.title: Specific Beats General
entries.summary: General rules describe the normal procedure, while a more specific feature, spell, item, or condition can change that procedure.
entries.whatItMeans: General rules describe the normal procedure, while a more specific feature, spell, item, or condition can change that procedure.
entries.exampleInPlay: The normal movement rule applies until a feature specifically allows movement without provoking an Opportunity Attack.
entries.whyItMatters: Many apparent contradictions are resolved by identifying which rule is more specific to the situation.
commonMistakes: A specific exception changes only what it says it changes; the rest of the general rule still applies.

entries.title: The d20 Test
entries.summary: When the outcome of an action is uncertain, roll a d20, add the relevant modifiers, and compare the total with a target number.
entries.whatItMeans: When the outcome of an action is uncertain, roll a d20, add the relevant modifiers, and compare the total with a target number.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character rolls 13, adds a +5 bonus, and reaches a total of 18 against a target number of 15.
entries.whyItMatters: Ability checks, attack rolls, and saving throws share the same basic engine even though each uses different bonuses and rules.
commonMistakes: A natural 20 or natural 1 does not automatically decide every kind of d20 roll; use the rule for the specific roll.

entries.title: Working Together
entries.summary: One creature can sometimes assist another with a task when the helper could reasonably attempt the task and the rules allow cooperation.
entries.whatItMeans: One creature can sometimes assist another with a task when the helper could reasonably attempt the task and the rules allow cooperation.
entries.exampleInPlay: One character steadies a ladder while another climbs, giving meaningful assistance to the attempt.
entries.whyItMatters: Assistance should follow the fiction rather than becoming an automatic source of Advantage on every check.
commonMistakes: A helper may need the same proficiency or capability when the task requires specialized knowledge.

entries.title: Ability Modifier
entries.summary: An ability modifier is derived from an ability score and is the number usually added to related rolls.
entries.whatItMeans: An ability modifier is derived from an ability score and is the number usually added to related rolls.
entries.exampleInPlay: A score of 14 or 15 gives a +2 modifier; a score of 8 or 9 gives a -1 modifier.
entries.whyItMatters: The modifier, rather than the full score, is used in most moment-to-moment play.

entries.title: Ability Score Generation
entries.summary: Ability scores can be entered manually or generated using an agreed method. The chosen numbers become the character's base Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma.
entries.whatItMeans: Ability scores can be entered manually or generated using an agreed method. The chosen numbers become the character's base Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma.
entries.exampleInPlay: Using 4d6 drop lowest, roll four six-sided dice, discard the lowest die, and total the other three for one score.
entries.whyItMatters: The generation method shapes a character's strengths and weaknesses before ancestry or background adjustments are applied.

entries.title: Ability Score Improvements and Feats
entries.summary: A class level may grant an Ability Score Improvement, a feat choice, or another option described by that edition and class.
entries.whatItMeans: A class level may grant an Ability Score Improvement, a feat choice, or another option described by that edition and class.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character uses the granted option to raise an ability score or select an eligible feat.
entries.whyItMatters: These choices shape long-term capability and must be recorded at the class level that granted them.
commonMistakes: An Ability Score Improvement is gained only when a class table or feature grants it.

entries.title: Ability Scores
entries.summary: The six ability scores describe a character's broad physical and mental capabilities.
entries.whatItMeans: The six ability scores describe a character's broad physical and mental capabilities.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Strength score of 16 produces a +3 Strength modifier.
entries.whyItMatters: Most character-sheet numbers eventually trace back to one of the six ability scores.

entries.title: Alignment
entries.summary: Alignment is a broad roleplaying description of a character's moral outlook and relationship with order, freedom, good, and evil.
entries.whatItMeans: Alignment is a broad roleplaying description of a character's moral outlook and relationship with order, freedom, good, and evil.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Lawful Good character might value duty and compassion, but still disagree with another Lawful Good character about the right action.
entries.whyItMatters: Alignment is a guide, not a script. Personality and choices remain more specific.
bestFor: Players using alignment as a roleplaying aid

entries.title: Background (2024)
entries.summary: A 2024 Background grants ability-score options, an Origin feat, skill proficiencies, a tool proficiency, and starting equipment.
entries.whatItMeans: A 2024 Background grants ability-score options, an Origin feat, skill proficiencies, a tool proficiency, and starting equipment.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Soldier chooses its permitted ability increases and gains the Background's listed feat and proficiencies.
entries.whyItMatters: Background now carries much of the mechanical weight that Race carried in the 2014 rules.

entries.title: Background Ability Scores (2024)
entries.summary: A 2024 Background offers three eligible abilities. Increase one by 2 and another by 1, or increase all three by 1, without raising a score above the normal character-creation limit.
entries.whatItMeans: A 2024 Background offers three eligible abilities. Increase one by 2 and another by 1, or increase all three by 1, without raising a score above the normal character-creation limit.
entries.exampleInPlay: Acolyte can place +2 in Wisdom and +1 in Charisma, or +1 in each of its three listed abilities.
entries.whyItMatters: These increases replace the old 2014 Race-based ability bonuses.

entries.title: Character Level and Class Level
entries.summary: Character level is the total of all class levels. Class level measures advancement in one specific class.
entries.whatItMeans: Character level is the total of all class levels. Class level measures advancement in one specific class.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Fighter 3 / Wizard 2 is a level 5 character, a level 3 Fighter, and a level 2 Wizard.
entries.whyItMatters: Many rules use one of these numbers specifically, so substituting the other can grant features too early or too late.

entries.title: Class Abilities and Feats
entries.summary: This section records the class features, feats, fighting styles, invocations, maneuvers, and other special abilities the character can use.
entries.whatItMeans: This section records the class features, feats, fighting styles, invocations, maneuvers, and other special abilities the character can use.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Fighter might record Action Surge and Second Wind, including how often each can be used.
entries.whyItMatters: Writing the feature name and its key limit makes the paper sheet much faster to use.

entries.title: Class and Level
entries.summary: A class describes the main adventuring path a character follows, while level measures progress in that class.
entries.whatItMeans: A class describes the main adventuring path a character follows, while level measures progress in that class.
entries.exampleInPlay: A level 3 Fighter has the features granted by the Fighter class through level 3.
entries.whyItMatters: Class and level determine most of a character's advancing abilities.

entries.title: Creature Size
entries.summary: Size categories describe how much space a creature controls and interact with movement, grappling, carrying, and other rules.
entries.whatItMeans: Size categories describe how much space a creature controls and interact with movement, grappling, carrying, and other rules.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Medium creature normally controls a 5-foot space in combat even though its body does not fill every part of that area.
entries.whyItMatters: Size is a rules category, not a precise measurement of height or weight.

entries.title: Experience Points
entries.summary: Experience Points, or XP, are one method for tracking progress toward the next character level.
entries.whatItMeans: Experience Points, or XP, are one method for tracking progress toward the next character level.
entries.exampleInPlay: When the campaign awards enough XP to reach the next threshold, the character gains a level.
entries.whyItMatters: Some campaigns use XP while others use milestone advancement.

entries.title: Gaining a Level
entries.summary: When a character gains a level, increase one class level and apply every feature, Hit Point change, and choice granted at that level.
entries.whatItMeans: When a character gains a level, increase one class level and apply every feature, Hit Point change, and choice granted at that level.
entries.exampleInPlay: A level 4 character advancing to level 5 applies the level 5 features of the chosen class and then checks character-level benefits.
entries.whyItMatters: Level advancement combines class-specific gains with benefits based on total character level.
commonMistakes: Do not increase every class when a multiclass character gains one character level.

entries.title: Heroic Inspiration (2024)
entries.summary: Heroic Inspiration lets a character reroll a die immediately after rolling it and use the new result. A character can hold only one Heroic Inspiration at a time.
entries.whatItMeans: Heroic Inspiration lets a character reroll a die immediately after rolling it and use the new result. A character can hold only one Heroic Inspiration at a time.
entries.exampleInPlay: After rolling poorly on a crucial save, spend Heroic Inspiration to reroll the die.
entries.whyItMatters: It provides a flexible second chance and should be recorded when gained or spent.

entries.title: Languages
entries.summary: Languages determine which spoken or written communication a character understands, as granted by origin, class, or other features.
entries.whatItMeans: Languages determine which spoken or written communication a character understands, as granted by origin, class, or other features.
entries.exampleInPlay: Two characters who share a language can communicate normally unless another effect interferes.
entries.whyItMatters: Language choices affect access to information without replacing social checks or roleplaying.

entries.title: Manual Ability Scores
entries.summary: Manual entry records scores chosen or generated outside the builder, subject to the rules and agreements of the table.
entries.whatItMeans: Manual entry records scores chosen or generated outside the builder, subject to the rules and agreements of the table.
entries.exampleInPlay: A player copies six scores from a paper character sheet into the builder.
entries.whyItMatters: Manual entry supports existing characters and house methods without forcing the builder to regenerate their numbers.
commonMistakes: The builder can record a value without proving that the campaign permits it.

entries.title: Multiclassing
entries.summary: Multiclassing divides character levels between two or more classes, subject to the edition's prerequisites and rules.
entries.whatItMeans: Multiclassing divides character levels between two or more classes, subject to the edition's prerequisites and rules.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Fighter 3 / Wizard 2 is a level 5 character with levels in two classes.
entries.whyItMatters: Multiclassing creates flexible combinations but can delay stronger features from a single class.

entries.title: Personality, Ideals, Bonds, and Flaws
entries.summary: These notes describe how a character behaves, what they believe, what they care about, and where they are vulnerable.
entries.whatItMeans: These notes describe how a character behaves, what they believe, what they care about, and where they are vulnerable.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character might be generous to strangers, devoted to a lost sibling, and dangerously unwilling to retreat.
entries.whyItMatters: Specific character details make roleplaying easier than relying on alignment alone.

entries.title: Point Buy
entries.summary: Point Buy creates ability scores by spending a fixed pool according to the edition’s cost table, normally before origin adjustments.
entries.whatItMeans: Point Buy creates ability scores by spending a fixed pool according to the edition’s cost table, normally before origin adjustments.
entries.exampleInPlay: A player spends more points to raise a score from 13 to 14 than to raise a low score by one point.
entries.whyItMatters: Point Buy offers more control than the Standard Array while keeping characters within a shared power range.
commonMistakes: Apply the point costs from the active edition rather than purchasing each increase at a flat one-point cost.

entries.title: Ready-to-Go Character Checklist
entries.summary: A ready-to-go character has the core choices and numbers needed to join play without requiring every personality or campaign detail to be finalized.
entries.whatItMeans: A ready-to-go character has the core choices and numbers needed to join play without requiring every personality or campaign detail to be finalized.
entries.exampleInPlay: The character has an edition, class, origin, ability scores, Hit Points, Armor Class, proficiencies, equipment, and any required choices recorded.
entries.whyItMatters: A clear minimum checklist lowers the barrier for new players while leaving room for the character to grow during play.

entries.title: Rolled Ability Scores
entries.summary: A group can generate ability scores with an agreed dice method, producing random strengths and weaknesses.
entries.whatItMeans: A group can generate ability scores with an agreed dice method, producing random strengths and weaknesses.
entries.exampleInPlay: A common method rolls four d6, discards the lowest die, and totals the other three for each score.
entries.whyItMatters: Rolling can create memorable characters, but everyone should agree on the method and how unusually weak or strong results are handled.

entries.title: Senses
entries.summary: Senses determine how a creature perceives its surroundings, including ordinary sight and special senses granted by a rule.
entries.whatItMeans: Senses determine how a creature perceives its surroundings, including ordinary sight and special senses granted by a rule.
entries.exampleInPlay: Darkvision may let a character see in darkness within a stated range, but it does not make every detail as clear as bright light.
entries.whyItMatters: Many combat and exploration rules depend on whether a creature can perceive a target or area.

entries.title: Species (2024)
entries.summary: In the 2024 rules, Species grants physical and supernatural traits such as speed, senses, resistances, and lineage choices. Ability-score increases come from Background instead.
entries.whatItMeans: In the 2024 rules, Species grants physical and supernatural traits such as speed, senses, resistances, and lineage choices. Ability-score increases come from Background instead.
entries.exampleInPlay: Choosing Elf grants Elf traits and asks for an Elven Lineage choice.
entries.whyItMatters: Keeping Species traits separate from Background ability scores is a central 2024 character-creation rule.

entries.title: Species Choices (2024)
entries.summary: Some 2024 Species require a choice such as lineage, ancestry, size, skill, feat, or spellcasting ability.
entries.whatItMeans: Some 2024 Species require a choice such as lineage, ancestry, size, skill, feat, or spellcasting ability.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Wood Elf lineage changes the character's Speed and grants its listed lineage magic.
entries.whyItMatters: These selections finish the Species package and should be recorded with the character.

entries.title: Standard Array
entries.summary: The Standard Array provides six fixed ability scores: 15, 14, 13, 12, 10, and 8, assigned once each.
entries.whatItMeans: The Standard Array provides six fixed ability scores: 15, 14, 13, 12, 10, and 8, assigned once each.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Fighter might assign 15 to Strength, 14 to Constitution, and place the remaining values according to the character concept.
entries.whyItMatters: It creates balanced characters quickly and avoids unusually high or low random results.

entries.title: Starting Equipment
entries.summary: A class and background provide starting equipment or a wealth option according to the active edition.
entries.whatItMeans: A class and background provide starting equipment or a wealth option according to the active edition.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character selects the listed class equipment choices and then adds the equipment provided by the background.
entries.whyItMatters: Starting equipment determines what a new character can use immediately and should not be confused with later purchases.

entries.title: Starting Hit Points
entries.summary: At level 1, a character’s class determines the base Hit Points, usually the maximum value of its Hit Die plus the Constitution modifier.
entries.whatItMeans: At level 1, a character’s class determines the base Hit Points, usually the maximum value of its Hit Die plus the Constitution modifier.
entries.exampleInPlay: A class with a d10 Hit Die and a +2 Constitution modifier begins with 12 Hit Points.
entries.whyItMatters: Correct starting Hit Points are essential because later level gains build on that total.

entries.title: Blindsight
entries.summary: Blindsight lets a creature perceive its surroundings within a stated range without relying on ordinary sight.
entries.whatItMeans: Blindsight lets a creature perceive its surroundings within a stated range without relying on ordinary sight.
entries.exampleInPlay: A creature with Blindsight can perceive a nearby invisible enemy within the sense’s range.
entries.whyItMatters: The sense has a limited range and does not necessarily reveal details beyond what its rule provides.

entries.title: Bright Light
entries.summary: Bright light allows ordinary vision within the illuminated area unless another effect obscures it.
entries.whatItMeans: Bright light allows ordinary vision within the illuminated area unless another effect obscures it.
entries.exampleInPlay: Daylight or a strong lamp creates an area where creatures can normally see clearly.
entries.whyItMatters: Light level determines whether vision-based rules apply before special senses are considered.

entries.title: Climbing
entries.summary: Climbing normally costs extra movement, and the Game Master can call for an ability check when the surface is difficult or dangerous.
entries.whatItMeans: Climbing normally costs extra movement, and the Game Master can call for an ability check when the surface is difficult or dangerous.
entries.exampleInPlay: Climbing 10 feet may consume 20 feet of movement before other modifiers are considered.
entries.whyItMatters: Tracking the extra movement keeps vertical terrain meaningful without requiring a roll for every ordinary ladder.

entries.title: Crawling
entries.summary: Crawling normally costs extra movement and often occurs while a creature is Prone or moving through a low space.
entries.whatItMeans: Crawling normally costs extra movement and often occurs while a creature is Prone or moving through a low space.
entries.exampleInPlay: A prone character crawls toward cover and spends additional movement for each foot travelled.
entries.whyItMatters: The movement cost makes dropping prone a tactical choice rather than free protection.

entries.title: Darkness
entries.summary: Darkness creates a heavily obscured area for creatures that cannot see through it with a special sense or effect.
entries.whatItMeans: Darkness creates a heavily obscured area for creatures that cannot see through it with a special sense or effect.
entries.exampleInPlay: A creature without Darkvision cannot rely on normal sight in an unlit underground chamber.
entries.whyItMatters: Darkness affects what can be seen, not whether a creature automatically knows that something exists.

entries.title: Darkvision
entries.summary: Darkvision lets a creature see within a stated range in darkness and dim light according to the active edition’s wording.
entries.whatItMeans: Darkvision lets a creature see within a stated range in darkness and dim light according to the active edition’s wording.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character with Darkvision can navigate an unlit corridor within the sense’s range, though colour or clarity may be limited.
entries.whyItMatters: Darkvision reduces the need for light but does not ignore every form of concealment or magical darkness.

entries.title: Dim Light
entries.summary: Dim light creates a lightly obscured area for creatures relying on normal sight.
entries.whatItMeans: Dim light creates a lightly obscured area for creatures relying on normal sight.
entries.exampleInPlay: Twilight or the edge of a torch’s illumination may impose the penalties associated with a lightly obscured area.
entries.whyItMatters: Dim light is not complete darkness, but it can still make visual observation less reliable.

entries.title: Falling
entries.summary: A creature that falls takes damage based on the distance fallen, up to the limit stated by the active edition, and usually lands Prone.
entries.whatItMeans: A creature that falls takes damage based on the distance fallen, up to the limit stated by the active edition, and usually lands Prone.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character pushed from a ledge takes falling damage on reaching the ground.
entries.whyItMatters: Falls can turn positioning into immediate danger even when no attack roll is involved.

entries.title: Food and Water
entries.summary: Characters need sufficient food and water during extended travel, with shortages causing the consequences defined by the active edition.
entries.whatItMeans: Characters need sufficient food and water during extended travel, with shortages causing the consequences defined by the active edition.
entries.exampleInPlay: A party crossing a remote region records rations and water for each day of the journey.
entries.whyItMatters: Resource pressure matters mainly during journeys where obtaining supplies is uncertain.

entries.title: Hiding
entries.summary: Hiding requires suitable circumstances and a Dexterity (Stealth) check, with the active edition determining how the hidden state is represented and discovered.
entries.whatItMeans: Hiding requires suitable circumstances and a Dexterity (Stealth) check, with the active edition determining how the hidden state is represented and discovered.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character moves behind opaque cover and attempts to remain unnoticed by nearby guards.
entries.whyItMatters: A successful Stealth check does not make a creature intangible; position, noise, line of sight, and enemy senses still matter.

entries.title: Jumping
entries.summary: Jump distance depends on Strength, available movement, and whether the jump has a running start, with the active edition defining the exact procedure.
entries.whatItMeans: Jump distance depends on Strength, available movement, and whether the jump has a running start, with the active edition defining the exact procedure.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character backs up for a running start before attempting to clear a gap.
entries.whyItMatters: A jump still uses movement, so the distance available on a turn can limit the attempt.
commonMistakes: A listed jump distance does not provide extra movement beyond what the creature has available.

entries.title: Marching Order
entries.summary: A travelling group can establish who is in front, middle, and rear so the Game Master can determine who notices or reaches a threat first.
entries.whatItMeans: A travelling group can establish who is in front, middle, and rear so the Game Master can determine who notices or reaches a threat first.
entries.exampleInPlay: The heavily armoured characters take the front while a scout watches the rear.
entries.whyItMatters: A marching order converts an abstract journey into clear positions when an encounter begins.

entries.title: Obscured Areas
entries.summary: Lightly and heavily obscured areas change how well creatures can see through foliage, fog, darkness, and similar visual interference.
entries.whatItMeans: Lightly and heavily obscured areas change how well creatures can see through foliage, fog, darkness, and similar visual interference.
entries.exampleInPlay: Dense fog can heavily obscure an area even during daylight.
entries.whyItMatters: Separating illumination from obstruction helps resolve situations where an area is bright but still impossible to see through.

entries.title: Searching
entries.summary: Searching is an active attempt to notice, locate, or understand something that is not immediately obvious.
entries.whatItMeans: Searching is an active attempt to notice, locate, or understand something that is not immediately obvious.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character examines a room for a concealed compartment rather than relying only on passive observation.
entries.whyItMatters: The approach determines whether Perception, Investigation, another ability, or no roll is appropriate.

entries.title: Suffocating
entries.summary: A creature can hold its breath for a limited time and then survives only a short number of rounds before dropping to 0 Hit Points.
entries.whatItMeans: A creature can hold its breath for a limited time and then survives only a short number of rounds before dropping to 0 Hit Points.
entries.exampleInPlay: A submerged character tracks remaining breath before the suffocation countdown begins.
entries.whyItMatters: Suffocation uses its own timing rules rather than ordinary damage each round.

entries.title: Swimming
entries.summary: Swimming normally costs extra movement unless a creature has an appropriate swimming speed or another rule changes the cost.
entries.whatItMeans: Swimming normally costs extra movement unless a creature has an appropriate swimming speed or another rule changes the cost.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character without a swimming speed spends additional movement to cross a calm pool.
entries.whyItMatters: A swimming speed and ordinary Speed are related but not interchangeable.

entries.title: Travel Pace
entries.summary: Travel pace describes how quickly a group moves over longer periods and may trade speed for stealth, awareness, or endurance.
entries.whatItMeans: Travel pace describes how quickly a group moves over longer periods and may trade speed for stealth, awareness, or endurance.
entries.exampleInPlay: A group chooses a slow pace to move cautiously through dangerous territory.
entries.whyItMatters: Travel pace is used for journeys rather than counting every five-foot square.

entries.title: Truesight
entries.summary: Truesight is a special sense that can perceive several forms of visual deception and transformation within a stated range.
entries.whatItMeans: Truesight is a special sense that can perceive several forms of visual deception and transformation within a stated range.
entries.exampleInPlay: A creature with Truesight may perceive the true form of a transformed creature within range.
entries.whyItMatters: Truesight is powerful but still limited by range and the exact benefits listed by the edition.

entries.title: Influence Action
entries.summary: The 2024 Influence action is used to alter a creature’s attitude or request behaviour through roleplay and an appropriate Charisma check when a roll is needed.
entries.whatItMeans: The 2024 Influence action is used to alter a creature’s attitude or request behaviour through roleplay and an appropriate Charisma check when a roll is needed.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character presents a reasonable request to a hesitant NPC and makes the check selected for the approach.
entries.whyItMatters: The action supplies a clearer procedure for uncertain social outcomes without turning NPCs into puppets.

entries.title: Insight and Social Checks
entries.summary: Insight helps interpret behaviour and intentions, while Charisma-based checks influence how a character presents a message or request.
entries.whatItMeans: Insight helps interpret behaviour and intentions, while Charisma-based checks influence how a character presents a message or request.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character uses Insight to notice that a merchant is nervous, then chooses how to respond.
entries.whyItMatters: Learning something about an NPC and persuading that NPC are separate goals and may use different checks.

entries.title: Social Interaction
entries.summary: Social interaction combines conversation, character goals, and sometimes ability checks when the outcome is uncertain.
entries.whatItMeans: Social interaction combines conversation, character goals, and sometimes ability checks when the outcome is uncertain.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character offers evidence and a promise of help while trying to convince a guard to allow entry.
entries.whyItMatters: A Charisma check does not replace the need to communicate an approach or make impossible demands reasonable.
commonMistakes: A successful social check influences an NPC within the situation; it is not mind control.

entries.title: Actions
entries.summary: On a turn, a creature normally takes one Action, such as Attack, Dash, Disengage, Dodge, Help, Hide, Influence, Magic, Ready, Search, Study, or Utilize.
entries.whatItMeans: On a turn, a creature normally takes one Action, such as Attack, Dash, Disengage, Dodge, Help, Hide, Influence, Magic, Ready, Search, Study, or Utilize.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character can use the Attack action to make attacks allowed by their features.
entries.whyItMatters: The Action is the main decision of most turns.

entries.title: Advantage and Disadvantage
entries.summary: With Advantage, roll two d20s and use the higher. With Disadvantage, roll two and use the lower. Multiple sources normally do not stack.
entries.whatItMeans: With Advantage, roll two d20s and use the higher. With Disadvantage, roll two and use the lower. Multiple sources normally do not stack.
entries.exampleInPlay: A hidden attacker with Advantage rolls two d20s and uses the higher result.
entries.whyItMatters: These rules change reliability without adding another numerical modifier.

entries.title: Armor Class
entries.summary: Armor Class, or AC, is the target number an attack roll must meet or exceed to hit.
entries.whatItMeans: Armor Class, or AC, is the target number an attack roll must meet or exceed to hit.
entries.exampleInPlay: An attack total of 17 hits AC 16.
entries.whyItMatters: Higher AC makes weapon and spell attacks less likely to hit.

entries.title: Attack Action
entries.summary: The Attack action allows a creature to make one attack, or more when a class feature or other rule says so.
entries.whatItMeans: The Attack action allows a creature to make one attack, or more when a class feature or other rule says so.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character with Extra Attack makes the number of attacks granted by that feature as part of one Attack action.
entries.whyItMatters: An attack is not always the same thing as the Attack action; some Bonus Actions, Reactions, and spells also make attacks.

entries.title: Attack Bonus
entries.summary: Attack Bonus is the total modifier added to an attack roll.
entries.whatItMeans: Attack Bonus is the total modifier added to an attack roll.
entries.exampleInPlay: A proficient Strength weapon attack might add Strength modifier plus Proficiency Bonus.
entries.whyItMatters: Recording the final bonus speeds up every attack.

entries.title: Attack Rolls
entries.summary: An attack roll is a d20 roll plus the relevant ability modifier and Proficiency Bonus when proficient.
entries.whatItMeans: An attack roll is a d20 roll plus the relevant ability modifier and Proficiency Bonus when proficient.
entries.exampleInPlay: A +5 attack bonus and a roll of 12 produce a total of 17.
entries.whyItMatters: Attack rolls are the most common way to resolve attempts to hit a target.

entries.title: Bonus Actions
entries.summary: A Bonus Action is an additional option available only when a feature, spell, or rule says it can be used as one.
entries.whatItMeans: A Bonus Action is an additional option available only when a feature, spell, or rule says it can be used as one.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Rogue might use Cunning Action as a Bonus Action.
entries.whyItMatters: You cannot invent a Bonus Action; a rule must grant one.

entries.title: Combat Sequence
entries.summary: Combat begins by establishing surprise or other opening conditions, determining initiative, and then taking turns in initiative order until the encounter ends.
entries.whatItMeans: Combat begins by establishing surprise or other opening conditions, determining initiative, and then taking turns in initiative order until the encounter ends.
entries.exampleInPlay: The group rolls initiative, the highest result takes the first turn, and the order repeats each round.
entries.whyItMatters: A shared sequence keeps simultaneous fictional action manageable at the table.

entries.title: Cover
entries.summary: Cover protects a target behind an obstacle. Half cover grants +2 AC and Dexterity saves, three-quarters cover grants +5, and total cover prevents direct targeting by many effects.
entries.whatItMeans: Cover protects a target behind an obstacle. Half cover grants +2 AC and Dexterity saves, three-quarters cover grants +5, and total cover prevents direct targeting by many effects.
entries.exampleInPlay: A low wall might provide half cover against an archer.
entries.whyItMatters: Using the environment can be as valuable as wearing better armor.

entries.title: Critical Hits
entries.summary: A critical hit normally rolls the attack's damage dice twice, then adds modifiers once.
entries.whatItMeans: A critical hit normally rolls the attack's damage dice twice, then adds modifiers once.
entries.exampleInPlay: A 1d8 weapon with a +3 modifier normally deals 2d8 + 3 on a critical hit.
entries.whyItMatters: Critical hits create sudden damage spikes.

entries.title: Damage Immunity
entries.summary: Damage immunity prevents damage of a specified type unless a more specific rule says otherwise.
entries.whatItMeans: Damage immunity prevents damage of a specified type unless a more specific rule says otherwise.
entries.exampleInPlay: A creature immune to poison damage takes no poison damage from an ordinary poison effect.
entries.whyItMatters: Immunity is different from resistance and can also apply separately to conditions.

entries.title: Damage Resistance
entries.summary: Resistance reduces damage of a specified type, normally by halving the damage after other modifiers specified by the rules.
entries.whatItMeans: Resistance reduces damage of a specified type, normally by halving the damage after other modifiers specified by the rules.
entries.exampleInPlay: A creature with fire resistance takes half of the fire damage from an effect.
entries.whyItMatters: Multiple sources of resistance to the same damage normally do not keep halving it.

entries.title: Damage Rolls
entries.summary: A damage roll determines how much HP an attack or effect removes after it hits or takes effect.
entries.whatItMeans: A damage roll determines how much HP an attack or effect removes after it hits or takes effect.
entries.exampleInPlay: A weapon might deal 1d8 plus an ability modifier.
entries.whyItMatters: Damage type and dice can interact with resistances, vulnerabilities, and critical hits.

entries.title: Damage Types
entries.summary: Damage types classify harm, allowing resistances, vulnerabilities, immunities, and other features to interact with it.
entries.whatItMeans: Damage types classify harm, allowing resistances, vulnerabilities, immunities, and other features to interact with it.
entries.exampleInPlay: A fire effect deals fire damage, which matters if the target resists or is immune to fire.
entries.whyItMatters: The type does not change the amount of damage unless another rule responds to that type.

entries.title: Damage Vulnerability
entries.summary: Vulnerability increases damage of a specified type, normally by doubling it after other modifiers specified by the rules.
entries.whatItMeans: Vulnerability increases damage of a specified type, normally by doubling it after other modifiers specified by the rules.
entries.exampleInPlay: A creature vulnerable to radiant damage takes twice the radiant damage from an effect.
entries.whyItMatters: Vulnerability can make damage type more important than the attack’s raw number of dice.

entries.title: Dash Action
entries.summary: The Dash action grants additional movement for the current turn based on the creature’s Speed after relevant modifiers.
entries.whatItMeans: The Dash action grants additional movement for the current turn based on the creature’s Speed after relevant modifiers.
entries.exampleInPlay: A creature with 30 feet of Speed Dashes and can normally move up to 60 feet during the turn.
entries.whyItMatters: Dash increases available movement rather than teleporting or creating a second turn.

entries.title: Death Saving Throws
entries.summary: At 0 HP, a character normally makes a Death Saving Throw at the start of each turn. Three successes stabilize; three failures cause death.
entries.whatItMeans: At 0 HP, a character normally makes a Death Saving Throw at the start of each turn. Three successes stabilize; three failures cause death.
entries.exampleInPlay: A roll of 10 or higher is normally a success. A natural 1 counts as two failures, while a natural 20 restores 1 HP.
entries.whyItMatters: Death saves create a short, dangerous window for allies to help.

entries.title: Difficult Terrain
entries.summary: Each foot of movement through difficult terrain normally costs an extra foot of movement.
entries.whatItMeans: Each foot of movement through difficult terrain normally costs an extra foot of movement.
entries.exampleInPlay: Moving 10 feet through difficult terrain usually costs 20 feet of Speed.
entries.whyItMatters: Terrain can make a short route more expensive than a longer clear route.

entries.title: Disengage Action
entries.summary: The Disengage action prevents the creature’s movement from provoking Opportunity Attacks for the rest of the turn.
entries.whatItMeans: The Disengage action prevents the creature’s movement from provoking Opportunity Attacks for the rest of the turn.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character Disengages before moving away from an adjacent enemy.
entries.whyItMatters: Disengage protects movement; it does not prevent other Reactions or hazards unless their rules depend on Opportunity Attacks.

entries.title: Dodge Action
entries.summary: The Dodge action makes the creature harder to hit and improves certain Dexterity saving throws until the stated timing ends, provided the creature can use the benefit.
entries.whatItMeans: The Dodge action makes the creature harder to hit and improves certain Dexterity saving throws until the stated timing ends, provided the creature can use the benefit.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character guarding a doorway Dodges instead of attacking, forcing visible attackers to roll with Disadvantage.
entries.whyItMatters: Dodge trades immediate offense for broad defense during a dangerous round.

entries.title: Dropping to 0 Hit Points
entries.summary: When a creature reaches 0 Hit Points, it may die immediately, fall Unconscious and begin making death saves, or follow a special rule for that creature.
entries.whatItMeans: When a creature reaches 0 Hit Points, it may die immediately, fall Unconscious and begin making death saves, or follow a special rule for that creature.
entries.exampleInPlay: A player character reduced to 0 Hit Points falls Unconscious and begins the death-saving-throw process unless the damage kills the character outright.
entries.whyItMatters: Zero Hit Points starts a new rules state rather than allowing Hit Points to become increasingly negative.

entries.title: Fighting with Two Weapons
entries.summary: Light weapons can enable an additional attack, with the action cost and modifier rules determined by the active edition and character features.
entries.whatItMeans: Light weapons can enable an additional attack, with the action cost and modifier rules determined by the active edition and character features.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character attacks with one light weapon and qualifies for the edition’s additional light-weapon attack.
entries.whyItMatters: The 2014 and 2024 procedures are different enough that they should never be combined.

entries.title: Grappling
entries.summary: Grappling restrains movement by applying the Grappled condition through the edition’s unarmed-strike or contest procedure.
entries.whatItMeans: Grappling restrains movement by applying the Grappled condition through the edition’s unarmed-strike or contest procedure.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character grabs an enemy to stop it from moving away.
entries.whyItMatters: The procedure and escape method differ between 2014 and 2024, so use the rule file for the active edition.

entries.title: Healing
entries.summary: Healing restores lost Hit Points up to a creature’s Hit Point maximum and normally has no effect on a dead creature unless a rule says otherwise.
entries.whatItMeans: Healing restores lost Hit Points up to a creature’s Hit Point maximum and normally has no effect on a dead creature unless a rule says otherwise.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character at 6 of 20 Hit Points receives 8 healing and rises to 14 Hit Points.
entries.whyItMatters: Healing does not create temporary Hit Points and excess healing is normally lost.

entries.title: Help Action
entries.summary: The Help action assists another creature with a task or attack when the stated conditions are met.
entries.whatItMeans: The Help action assists another creature with a task or attack when the stated conditions are met.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character distracts an enemy so an ally gains the Help benefit on an attack against that enemy.
entries.whyItMatters: Help requires proximity or a plausible method and affects the next qualifying attempt rather than every ally indefinitely.

entries.title: Hide Action
entries.summary: The Hide action is the combat procedure for attempting to become hidden when circumstances allow it.
entries.whatItMeans: The Hide action is the combat procedure for attempting to become hidden when circumstances allow it.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character moves behind total cover and uses the Hide action before an enemy can locate them.
entries.whyItMatters: The action starts an attempt; whether the creature remains hidden depends on the roll, position, senses, and later behaviour.

entries.title: Hit Dice
entries.summary: Hit Dice are class-based dice used for calculating HP and commonly for recovering HP during a Short Rest.
entries.whatItMeans: Hit Dice are class-based dice used for calculating HP and commonly for recovering HP during a Short Rest.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Fighter normally uses a d10 Hit Die for Fighter levels.
entries.whyItMatters: Multiclass characters may track more than one Hit Die type.

entries.title: Hit Points
entries.summary: Hit Points, or HP, measure how much damage a character can sustain before dropping to 0 HP.
entries.whatItMeans: Hit Points, or HP, measure how much damage a character can sustain before dropping to 0 HP.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character at 12 HP who takes 7 damage has 5 HP left.
entries.whyItMatters: HP is the clearest measure of immediate endurance in combat.

entries.title: Initiative
entries.summary: Initiative determines turn order when combat begins.
entries.whatItMeans: Initiative determines turn order when combat begins.
entries.exampleInPlay: Each participant rolls initiative, usually using Dexterity.
entries.whyItMatters: Acting earlier can change positioning and protect allies.

entries.title: Instant Death
entries.summary: Massive excess damage can kill a creature immediately when the remaining damage after reaching 0 Hit Points meets the rule’s threshold.
entries.whatItMeans: Massive excess damage can kill a creature immediately when the remaining damage after reaching 0 Hit Points meets the rule’s threshold.
entries.exampleInPlay: A badly wounded character takes enough damage that the excess equals or exceeds the Hit Point maximum.
entries.whyItMatters: The rule makes extremely powerful blows dangerous even before death saving throws can occur.

entries.title: Interacting with Objects
entries.summary: A turn can include limited interaction with nearby objects, while more involved use may require an Action under the active edition.
entries.whatItMeans: A turn can include limited interaction with nearby objects, while more involved use may require an Action under the active edition.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character draws a weapon while moving, but operating a complicated mechanism may require the appropriate Action.
entries.whyItMatters: Separating simple interaction from a full Action keeps ordinary movement fluid without making every object free to manipulate.

entries.title: Knocking a Creature Out
entries.summary: When a qualifying melee attack reduces a creature to 0 Hit Points, the attacker can choose to leave it Unconscious and stable instead of killing it.
entries.whatItMeans: When a qualifying melee attack reduces a creature to 0 Hit Points, the attacker can choose to leave it Unconscious and stable instead of killing it.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character drops a guard to 0 Hit Points with a melee attack and chooses to knock the guard out.
entries.whyItMatters: The choice supports capture and restraint without creating a separate nonlethal damage pool.

entries.title: Long Range
entries.summary: A ranged weapon can attack beyond its normal range and up to its long range with Disadvantage; beyond long range, the attack cannot be made.
entries.whatItMeans: A ranged weapon can attack beyond its normal range and up to its long range with Disadvantage; beyond long range, the attack cannot be made.
entries.exampleInPlay: A weapon listed as 80/320 attacks normally within 80 feet and with Disadvantage beyond 80 feet up to 320 feet.
entries.whyItMatters: The two range numbers are thresholds, not bonuses added to the attack roll.

entries.title: Melee Attacks
entries.summary: Melee attacks target creatures within the weapon or effect's reach.
entries.whatItMeans: Melee attacks target creatures within the weapon or effect's reach.
entries.exampleInPlay: A longsword normally attacks a target within 5 feet.
entries.whyItMatters: Melee positioning can expose a character to retaliation and opportunity attacks.

entries.title: Movement
entries.summary: A creature can move up to its Speed during its turn and can split that movement around actions when permitted.
entries.whatItMeans: A creature can move up to its Speed during its turn and can split that movement around actions when permitted.
entries.exampleInPlay: Move 10 feet, attack, then move the remaining 20 feet of a 30-foot Speed.
entries.whyItMatters: Movement is separate from the Action but can trigger hazards or opportunity attacks.

entries.title: Opportunity Attacks
entries.summary: An opportunity attack is a Reaction triggered when a visible enemy willingly leaves your reach without using a rule that prevents it.
entries.whatItMeans: An opportunity attack is a Reaction triggered when a visible enemy willingly leaves your reach without using a rule that prevents it.
entries.exampleInPlay: A creature moving away from a sword-wielding enemy may provoke an attack before leaving reach.
entries.whyItMatters: Threatened movement can shape positioning and escape choices.

entries.title: Passive Perception
entries.summary: Passive Perception represents what a character notices without making an active roll.
entries.whatItMeans: Passive Perception represents what a character notices without making an active roll.
entries.exampleInPlay: A hidden danger can be compared against the character's Passive Perception.
entries.whyItMatters: It lets the GM resolve awareness without repeatedly asking for rolls.

entries.title: Proficiency Bonus
entries.summary: Proficiency Bonus is added when the character is trained in a save, skill, weapon, tool, or other rule that grants proficiency.
entries.whatItMeans: Proficiency Bonus is added when the character is trained in a save, skill, weapon, tool, or other rule that grants proficiency.
entries.exampleInPlay: A proficient skill with a +3 ability modifier and +2 Proficiency Bonus has a +5 total.
entries.whyItMatters: It scales with total character level and powers many core calculations.

entries.title: Ranged Attacks
entries.summary: Ranged attacks target at a distance and normally use the weapon or spell's listed range.
entries.whatItMeans: Ranged attacks target at a distance and normally use the weapon or spell's listed range.
entries.exampleInPlay: A bow can attack a distant target, with penalties or restrictions beyond normal range.
entries.whyItMatters: Range allows safer positioning but can be affected by cover and nearby enemies.

entries.title: Ranged Attacks in Close Combat
entries.summary: A ranged attack can suffer Disadvantage when a hostile creature is close enough and able to interfere, according to the edition’s rule.
entries.whatItMeans: A ranged attack can suffer Disadvantage when a hostile creature is close enough and able to interfere, according to the edition’s rule.
entries.exampleInPlay: An archer standing beside an active enemy attacks a distant target with Disadvantage.

entries.title: Combining Magical Effects
entries.summary: Different magical effects can usually overlap, while repeated instances of the same named effect follow the edition’s rule for overlapping duration and benefits.
entries.whatItMeans: Different magical effects can usually overlap, while repeated instances of the same named effect follow the edition’s rule for overlapping duration and benefits.
entries.exampleInPlay: Two castings of the same spell do not necessarily double every benefit, even when both durations continue.
entries.whyItMatters: This prevents identical effects from multiplying beyond what their rules intend.

entries.title: Concentration
entries.summary: A creature can normally concentrate on only one effect at a time. Taking damage can require a Constitution save with DC 10 or half the damage taken, whichever is higher.
entries.whatItMeans: A creature can normally concentrate on only one effect at a time. Taking damage can require a Constitution save with DC 10 or half the damage taken, whichever is higher.
entries.exampleInPlay: Taking 22 damage while concentrating normally calls for a DC 11 Constitution save.
entries.whyItMatters: Starting another Concentration effect ends the first, so timing matters.

entries.title: Costly and Consumed Components
entries.summary: A material component with a listed cost must be available, and a component is used up only when the spell says it is consumed.
entries.whatItMeans: A material component with a listed cost must be available, and a component is used up only when the spell says it is consumed.
entries.exampleInPlay: A diamond with a stated value cannot be replaced by a focus, and it disappears only if the spell says the diamond is consumed.
entries.whyItMatters: Cost and consumption are separate restrictions and should be tracked separately.

entries.title: Expending a Spell Slot
entries.summary: Casting a leveled spell normally expends one spell slot of the spell’s level or higher unless a rule provides another method.
entries.whatItMeans: Casting a leveled spell normally expends one spell slot of the spell’s level or higher unless a rule provides another method.
entries.exampleInPlay: Casting a 2nd-level spell with a 3rd-level slot expends the 3rd-level slot.
entries.whyItMatters: The slot is the resource spent; the prepared or known spell normally remains available to cast again if another slot is available.

entries.title: Magic Action
entries.summary: The 2024 Magic action is used to cast a spell with that casting time or activate a magical feature or item that requires the action.
entries.whatItMeans: The 2024 Magic action is used to cast a spell with that casting time or activate a magical feature or item that requires the action.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character takes the Magic action to cast a spell whose casting time is an Action.
entries.whyItMatters: Calling out the Magic action separates magical activity from the Attack, Utilize, and other actions.

entries.title: Material Components
entries.summary: A material component requires the listed object, a component pouch, or an eligible spellcasting focus unless the component has a stated cost or is consumed.
entries.whatItMeans: A material component requires the listed object, a component pouch, or an eligible spellcasting focus unless the component has a stated cost or is consumed.
entries.exampleInPlay: A focus replaces an ordinary pinch of material but not a gem with a listed gold-piece value.
entries.whyItMatters: The component line determines what must be held or available when the spell is cast.

entries.title: Multiclass Spellcasting
entries.summary: A multiclass character may combine certain class levels to determine spell slots while still preparing or knowing spells separately for each class.
entries.whatItMeans: A multiclass character may combine certain class levels to determine spell slots while still preparing or knowing spells separately for each class.
entries.exampleInPlay: A multiclass character calculates the shared slot table, then checks each class independently for which spells can be prepared or known.
entries.whyItMatters: Combined slots do not grant access to higher-level class spells before the relevant class can prepare or know them.

entries.title: One Spell Slot per Turn
entries.summary: In the 2024 rules, a creature can expend only one spell slot during a turn, regardless of which actions or reactions are used on that turn.
entries.whatItMeans: In the 2024 rules, a creature can expend only one spell slot during a turn, regardless of which actions or reactions are used on that turn.
entries.exampleInPlay: After expending a spell slot for one spell on the turn, the character can still cast a cantrip that uses no slot if the action economy allows it.
entries.whyItMatters: The restriction follows slot expenditure rather than the 2014 Bonus-Action spell procedure.

entries.title: Prepared and Known Spells
entries.summary: A class or feature determines which spells a character knows or prepares and how that list can change.
entries.whatItMeans: A class or feature determines which spells a character knows or prepares and how that list can change.
entries.exampleInPlay: A prepared caster selects spells from the class list according to its preparation rule.
entries.whyItMatters: Spell slots are useless without an available spell to cast with them.

entries.title: Ritual Casting
entries.summary: A spell with the Ritual tag can be cast as a ritual by a character whose feature allows it, adding time but usually avoiding a spell-slot cost.
entries.whatItMeans: A spell with the Ritual tag can be cast as a ritual by a character whose feature allows it, adding time but usually avoiding a spell-slot cost.
entries.exampleInPlay: A ritual-capable caster can cast a prepared ritual without spending a slot by taking the extra time.
entries.whyItMatters: Rituals preserve slots when time is available.

entries.title: Somatic Components
entries.summary: A somatic component requires a free hand or a hand permitted by the spellcasting rules to perform precise gestures.
entries.whatItMeans: A somatic component requires a free hand or a hand permitted by the spellcasting rules to perform precise gestures.
entries.exampleInPlay: A caster may need to free a hand before casting a spell with a somatic component.
entries.whyItMatters: Equipment choices can affect whether the caster can supply the required gestures.

entries.title: Sorcery Points and Magical Pools
entries.summary: Some classes and features use a separate pool of points to modify spells or activate magical abilities.
entries.whatItMeans: Some classes and features use a separate pool of points to modify spells or activate magical abilities.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Sorcerer records current Sorcery Points and the Metamagic options that spend them.
entries.whyItMatters: Clear resource tracking prevents accidental overuse.

entries.title: Spell Attack Bonus
entries.summary: Spell Attack Bonus is added to spell attack rolls and normally equals Proficiency Bonus plus the relevant spellcasting ability modifier.
entries.whatItMeans: Spell Attack Bonus is added to spell attack rolls and normally equals Proficiency Bonus plus the relevant spellcasting ability modifier.
entries.exampleInPlay: A +3 spellcasting modifier and +2 Proficiency Bonus produce a +5 spell attack bonus.
entries.whyItMatters: Attack spells use this number instead of a weapon attack bonus.

entries.title: Spell Components
entries.summary: Spell components describe what casting requires: verbal words, somatic gestures, and material objects or a spellcasting focus.
entries.whatItMeans: Spell components describe what casting requires: verbal words, somatic gestures, and material objects or a spellcasting focus.
entries.exampleInPlay: A spell with somatic components may require a free hand unless another rule allows the hand to hold a focus or material component.
entries.whyItMatters: Components determine whether a character can cast in unusual situations.

entries.title: Spell Duration
entries.summary: Duration states how long a spell lasts, such as Instantaneous, 1 minute, or until dispelled. Some durations require Concentration.
entries.whatItMeans: Duration states how long a spell lasts, such as Instantaneous, 1 minute, or until dispelled. Some durations require Concentration.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Concentration spell lasting up to 1 minute ends early if Concentration breaks.
entries.whyItMatters: Tracking duration prevents effects from lasting too long or ending too early.

entries.title: Spell Level
entries.summary: Every spell has a level from 0 to 9 that indicates its general power and the slot normally required to cast it.
entries.whatItMeans: Every spell has a level from 0 to 9 that indicates its general power and the slot normally required to cast it.
entries.exampleInPlay: A 3rd-level spell normally requires a spell slot of 3rd level or higher.
entries.whyItMatters: Spell level is not the same as character level or class level.

entries.title: Spell Lists
entries.summary: A spell list identifies which spells a class, feature, or other rule can choose from.
entries.whatItMeans: A spell list identifies which spells a class, feature, or other rule can choose from.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Wizard chooses from the Wizard spell list unless another feature expands the available choices.
entries.whyItMatters: Having a spell slot does not by itself grant access to every spell of that level.

entries.title: Spell Range
entries.summary: Range states where a spell can originate or which targets it can affect. Self, Touch, and measured distances use different targeting limits.
entries.whatItMeans: Range states where a spell can originate or which targets it can affect. Self, Touch, and measured distances use different targeting limits.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Touch spell normally requires the caster to reach the target.
entries.whyItMatters: Range determines whether positioning permits the spell at all.

entries.title: Spell Save DC
entries.summary: Spell Save DC is the target number a creature must meet or exceed on a saving throw against the character's spell.
entries.whatItMeans: Spell Save DC is the target number a creature must meet or exceed on a saving throw against the character's spell.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Spell Save DC of 14 requires a saving throw total of 14 or higher to succeed.
entries.whyItMatters: A higher DC makes save-based spells harder to resist.

entries.title: Spell Slots
entries.summary: Spell slots are resources spent to cast leveled spells. A slot's level must be at least the spell's level.
entries.whatItMeans: Spell slots are resources spent to cast leveled spells. A slot's level must be at least the spell's level.
entries.exampleInPlay: A 1st-level spell can be cast using a 1st-level or higher slot.
entries.whyItMatters: Slots are a spellcaster's primary limited resource.

entries.title: Spell Targets
entries.summary: A spell specifies what it can target, how many targets it can affect, and whether the caster must see or reach them.
entries.whatItMeans: A spell specifies what it can target, how many targets it can affect, and whether the caster must see or reach them.
entries.exampleInPlay: A spell that targets one creature cannot normally be redirected to an unattended object.
entries.whyItMatters: The target line is a rule, not merely descriptive wording.

entries.title: Spellcasting
entries.summary: Spellcasting uses class or feature rules to cast spells, usually involving a spellcasting ability, components, range, duration, and sometimes spell slots.
entries.whatItMeans: Spellcasting uses class or feature rules to cast spells, usually involving a spellcasting ability, components, range, duration, and sometimes spell slots.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Wizard uses Intelligence for Wizard spells.
entries.whyItMatters: Recording the key statistics prevents repeated rulebook searches.

entries.title: Spellcasting Ability
entries.summary: A spellcasting ability is the ability used to calculate a character's spell attack bonus and Spell Save DC for a particular source of magic.
entries.whatItMeans: A spellcasting ability is the ability used to calculate a character's spell attack bonus and Spell Save DC for a particular source of magic.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Cleric normally uses Wisdom for Cleric spells.
entries.whyItMatters: Multiclass characters can have more than one spellcasting ability.

entries.title: Spellcasting Focus
entries.summary: An eligible spellcasting focus can replace ordinary material components for spells cast through the feature that permits that focus.
entries.whatItMeans: An eligible spellcasting focus can replace ordinary material components for spells cast through the feature that permits that focus.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Cleric uses a holy symbol as the material component for a spell that has no costly or consumed component.
entries.whyItMatters: A focus is not a universal substitute for every spell or every class.

entries.title: Verbal Components
entries.summary: A verbal component requires the caster to produce the spell’s required sounds and cannot be supplied while the caster is unable to speak as required.
entries.whatItMeans: A verbal component requires the caster to produce the spell’s required sounds and cannot be supplied while the caster is unable to speak as required.
entries.exampleInPlay: A caster inside an effect that prevents sound cannot provide a verbal component.
entries.whyItMatters: Verbal components make many spells noticeable and vulnerable to effects that prevent speech or sound.
